question: What is the term for the entire group of people a researcher wants to study?
explanation: The target population is the complete group of individuals the researcher is interested in and wants to apply their findings to. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T7#BMP225_U2_T7_h1)

question: Why do midwives studying a health topic usually look at a sample instead of the whole population?

options.A: It is impossible to study everyone due to limited time and money.
options.B: Larger groups always give completely inaccurate medical data.
options.C: Ethics committees forbid studying more than fifty patients at once.
options.D: Hospital management prefers smaller administrative workloads.

explanation: Limited resources like funding, staff, and time make studying an entire population impractical, so researchers use a representative sample instead. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T7#BMP225_U2_T7_h1)

question: What happens if a researcher just guesses the number of participants needed for a study?

options.A: The research paper will be published in international journals faster.
options.B: The ethical board will automatically approve the research protocol.
options.C: Data analysis software will refuse to process the collected information.
options.D: The study may not have enough participants to find true clinical differences.

explanation: Guessing sample sizes often results in studies that are too small to detect genuine medical effects or relationships. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T7#BMP225_U2_T7_h2)

question: What two things must a researcher balance when figuring out how many participants are needed?

options.A: Hospital budget constraints with personal salary desires
options.B: Morning shift data collection with night shift records
options.C: Male participants equally with female participants
options.D: Statistical needs with available resources and logistics

explanation: Sample size planning requires weighing mathematical requirements for accuracy against practical limits like money, time, and staffing. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T7#BMP225_U2_T7_h2)

question: What factor describes how much data points vary or spread out within a study group?
explanation: Variance measures how much individual data points differ from the average, and higher variability means a larger sample is needed for accuracy. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T7#BMP225_U2_T7_h3)

question: How does expecting a very small clinical difference affect the number of study participants needed?

options.A: It forces the hospital to change its standard operating procedures.
options.B: It requires a larger sample size to detect the subtle change.
options.C: It eliminates the need for any statistical power calculations.
options.D: It allows the researcher to use a much smaller group of patients.

explanation: Subtle differences are harder to spot, so researchers need more participants to ensure the finding is real and not just random chance. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T7#BMP225_U2_T7_h3)

question: What is another name for a Type I error in research statistics?
explanation: A Type I error happens when a researcher mistakenly claims a significant effect exists when it is actually not there. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T7#BMP225_U2_T7_h4)

question: What does a statistical power level of 80% mean for a study?

options.A: There is an 80% chance that the research funding will cover all costs.
options.B: Only 20% of the target population has the medical condition of interest.
options.C: There is an 80% chance of detecting a real clinical difference if it exists.
options.D: Eighty percent of the participants will complete the entire study protocol.

explanation: Statistical power is the probability that a study will successfully spot a genuine effect when one is actually present. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T7#BMP225_U2_T7_h4)

question: What does the term 'attrition' mean in clinical research?

options.A: Errors made by data entry clerks during statistical analysis
options.B: Participants dropping out or withdrawing before the study ends
options.C: The natural decay of paper records kept in storage rooms
options.D: The gradual reduction of hospital equipment budgets over time

explanation: Attrition means losing study participants over time because they move, withdraw consent, or cannot be reached for follow-up. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T7#BMP225_U2_T7_h5)

question: If a researcher needs 200 postnatal mothers to finish a study and expects a 15% dropout rate, how many should be recruited at the start?
explanation: To make sure 200 people complete the study even if 15 percent drop out, divide 200 by 0.85, which gives about 235 initial recruits. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T7#BMP225_U2_T7_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a good way to decide on a study sample size?

options.A: Consulting a biostatistician during the design phase
options.B: Taking whichever patients happen to walk into the clinic for two weeks
options.C: Using standard mathematical formulas based on expected effect size
options.D: Accounting for anticipated dropouts based on previous similar studies

explanation: Choosing whoever is easily available without mathematical backing often produces biased samples that do not truly represent the population. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T7#BMP225_U2_T7_h6)

question: Why is relying only on rigid rules of thumb from old textbooks risky for modern research?

options.A: Hospital ethics committees automatically reject any reference to books.
options.B: Textbooks from past decades are illegal to reference in thesis writing.
options.C: Modern computers can only process samples larger than ten thousand people.
options.D: Different research questions and designs require unique statistical parameters.

explanation: Every study has different variables and goals, meaning a simple blanket rule rarely fits every specific clinical situation accurately. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T7#BMP225_U2_T7_h6)
